title: TrafficMirror: The Definitive Guide to Zero-Risk Production Traffic Shadowing and Automated Regression Testing
summary:
In modern distributed systems, testing in staging environments is fundamentally broken. Synthetic load generators, mock services, and sanitized database dumps fail to replicate the sheer entropy, concurrency spikes, edge-case payloads, and network anomalies inherent to live production environments. As systems grow in complexity, the phrase "it worked in staging" has transitioned from an industry joke to a multi-million-dollar operational liability.

Deploying untested regressions, unoptimized database queries, or breaking schema updates directly to production endangers revenue and brand equity. While blue-green and canary deployments mitigate some blast radiuses, they still expose a percentage of live users to potential failures.

Enter TrafficMirror: the next-generation, high-throughput, cloud-native traffic replication, shadowing, and real-time diffing engine.

Designed for Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), Platform Architects, and Enterprise Engineering teams, TrafficMirror transparently duplicates real-world HTTP, gRPC, and raw TCP traffic at the network layer and replays it asynchronously against candidate clusters—delivering zero-latency-impact validation before a single user ever touches new code.

1. The Architectural Impasse of Modern QA

Traditional verification pipelines rely on three outdated assumptions:

  1. Mocks represent reality: Handcrafted mocks drift from production API contracts within days of deployment.
  2. Synthetic tests catch edge cases: Synthetic testing tools simulate expected behaviors, whereas production traffic is defined by unexpected behaviors.
  3. Canaries isolate risk entirely: A canary deployment routing 1% of live traffic to a faulty microservice still subjects hundreds or thousands of paying users to 500-series errors or corrupted state transitions. 
[ Traditional Canary Deployments ]
User Request ---> [ Ingress Router ] 
                        │
                        ├── (99%) ──> [ Production Service v1.0 ] (Safe)
                        └── (1%)  ──> [ Canary Service v1.1 ]    (Real Users Impacted on Failure)

[ TrafficMirror Architecture ]
User Request ---> [ Ingress / eBPF Tap ]
                        │
                        ├── (Primary Sync) ────> [ Production Service v1.0 ] ---> Response to User
                        │
                        └── (Async Shadow) ───> [ TrafficMirror Engine ]
                                                        │
                                                        ├── (Sanitization / PII Scrub)
                                                        └── (Zero-Impact Replay) ──> [ Candidate Service v1.1 ]
                                                                                              │
                                                                [ Diff Engine & Analytics ] <─┘

TrafficMirror inverts this paradigm. By tapping directly into the network data plane (via eBPF hooks or high-performance sidecars), TrafficMirror duplicates inbound requests, scrubs sensitive data at the wire level, and asynchronously streams the payload to non-production clusters. Responses from the target services are intercepted, compared, and discarded—guaranteeing that zero live users are affected by regressions, memory leaks, or unhandled exceptions.

2. Core Technical Architecture of TrafficMirror

TrafficMirror is engineered in Rust to achieve single-digit microsecond overhead, leveraging memory safety, lock-free concurrency, and asynchronous I/O primitives.

A. The Capture Plane: Kernel-Level Packet Interception

Instead of routing production traffic through heavy, unoptimized application-level proxies, TrafficMirror utilizes eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter) at the Linux socket layer (sockops / tc egress/ingress hooks).

When a TCP handshake completes on a designated port, TrafficMirror clones the sk_buff buffer at the kernel level. This ensures:

  • Zero context-switching penalties: The kernel duplicates the data stream without traversing user-space boundaries twice.
  • No latency impact on the primary path: The downstream client receives the response directly from the stable upstream service, completely decoupled from shadow stream execution.

B. Payload Sanitization & Dynamic PII Redaction

Replaying production payloads into staging environments presents immediate compliance hurdles (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS). TrafficMirror features a zero-allocation streaming parser that identifies and transforms sensitive fields on the fly:

// Original Inbound Payload (Production)
{
  "user_id": "usr_998124",
  "credit_card": "4532-7598-1234-5678",
  "cvv": "882",
  "auth_token": "bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..."
}

// Replayed Payload to Candidate Cluster
{
  "user_id": "usr_998124",
  "credit_card": "4532-XXXX-XXXX-5678",
  "cvv": "000",
  "auth_token": "test-mock-token-session-valid"
}

Dynamic mutation rules allow teams to inject deterministic synthetic test credentials, swap out production API tokens, and rewrite host headers without incurring serialization bottlenecks.

C. The Diffing & Drift Engine

Replaying traffic is useless without granular validation. TrafficMirror collects the responses from both the primary (v1.0) and shadow (v1.1) environments, piping them into a distributed diffing pipeline.

The engine accounts for:

  • Timestamp Drift: Dynamic fields like generated_at, nonce, or trace_id are automatically ignored using structural AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) matching.
  • JSON Structure vs. Whitespace: Semantic comparisons instead of raw string checks.
  • Latency & Resource Profiling: Measuring p95, p99, and p99.9 latency variance between builds under identical concurrency.

3. Production Deployment: Kubernetes & Cloud-Native Integration

TrafficMirror is designed to fit directly into your existing infrastructure stack. Below is a production-grade Kubernetes Custom Resource Definition (CRD) detailing a typical deployment shadowing a critical payment gateway service.

apiVersion: trafficmirror.io/v1alpha1
kind: MirrorSession
metadata:
  name: payment-service-shadow
  namespace: core-banking
spec:
  source:
    service: payment-gateway
    port: 8080
    selector:
      app: payment-gateway
      tier: api
  target:
    service: payment-gateway-candidate
    namespace: core-banking-staging
    port: 8080
  captureStrategy:
    mode: eBPF
    sampleRate: "100%"
    bufferLimitBytes: 104857600 # 100MB ring-buffer
  sanitization:
    headers:
      - key: "Authorization"
        action: "Replace"
        value: "Bearer staging-test-token"
    jsonBody:
      - jsonPath: "$.payment.pan"
        action: "Mask"
        pattern: "^[0-9]{12}"
        replacement: "XXXXXXXXXXXX"
      - jsonPath: "$.payment.cvv"
        action: "Set"
        value: "000"
  analysis:
    diffEngine:
      enabled: true
      ignoreFields:
        - "$.meta.response_timestamp"
        - "$.meta.request_id"
    alerting:
      errorThresholdPercentage: 0.05
      latencyDriftP99Ms: 25

4. Key Engineering Use Cases

1. Monolith-to-Microservice Deconstruction

Refactoring legacy codebases (such as Java or Ruby monoliths) into modern Go, Rust, or Node.js microservices is fraught with hidden behavioral dependencies. TrafficMirror lets you route live monolith requests to the new service concurrently, proving 100% behavioral parity over billions of real-world requests before deprecating legacy systems.

2. High-Risk Database Migrations

Upgrading from Postgres 12 to 16, swapping an ORM, or migrating from relational tables to an event-sourced distributed store often yields unexpected index misses and deadlocks. By mirroring read/write traffic (with writes redirected to an isolated sandbox DB), TrafficMirror reveals indexing bottlenecks, query plan regressions, and lock contentions under actual peak load.

3. Machine Learning & LLM Proxy Evaluation

When upgrading fine-tuned models or inference pipelines, static test datasets fail to represent the infinite variety of prompt inputs. Mirroring live prompt streams to candidate inference models allows evaluation of hallucinations, token efficiency, response latencies, and output formats at enterprise scale.

5. Economic ROI: Eliminating the Failure Tax

Downtime and software defects carry a massive financial toll:

  • The average cost of enterprise IT downtime is estimated at $5,600 to $9,000 per minute.
  • Discovering a critical defect in production costs up to 100x more than detecting it in pre-production.
  • Engineering hours wasted on manual post-mortems, rollbacks, and hotfixes siphon capital away from core product innovation. 
+------------------------------------+--------------------------+--------------------------+
| Metric                             | Traditional Deployment   | With TrafficMirror       |
+------------------------------------+--------------------------+--------------------------+
| Regression Escape Rate             | 8% - 15%                 | < 0.1%                   |
| Staging Environment Maintenance    | 20-30 hrs/month          | < 2 hrs/month            |
| Deployment Blast Radius           | Live users impacted      | Zero real-user impact    |
| Time-to-Confidence for Major DFs   | Weeks of manual QA       | Hours of dark traffic    |
+------------------------------------+--------------------------+--------------------------+

TrafficMirror transforms engineering confidence from an intuitive guess into a mathematical certainty. By validating your candidate releases against identical, real-world data patterns, you compress release cycles from bi-weekly sprints to continuous, risk-free hourly deployments.

6. Get Started with TrafficMirror Today

The era of trusting artificial staging environments and hoping for the best during production deploys is over. Elevate your engineering organization's velocity, slash MTTR to zero, and guarantee five-nines availability with automated, real-time traffic mirroring.

Designed for Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), Platform Architects, and Enterprise Engineering teams, TrafficMirror transparently duplicates real-world HTTP, gRPC, and raw TCP traffic at the network layer and replays it asynchronously against candidate clusters—delivering zero-latency-impact validation before a single user ever touches new code.

Traditional verification pipelines rely on three outdated assumptions:

TrafficMirror is engineered in Rust to achieve single-digit microsecond overhead, leveraging memory safety, lock-free concurrency, and asynchronous I/O primitives.

Instead of routing production traffic through heavy, unoptimized application-level proxies, TrafficMirror utilizes eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter) at the Linux socket layer (sockops / tc egress/ingress hooks).

title: How to Preview a Weave Router Benchmark Run Before Launch
summary:
A benchmark launch can fan out across tasks, attempts, and model routes. Before spending model or sandbox time, inspect the exact plan.

Weave Router's public weave-bench CLI has a --dry-run option for that step. It resolves the benchmark manifest, builds one Harbor command per comparison arm, prints the commands and version pins, then exits before launching any Harbor jobs. In this walkthrough, the plan selects one Terminal-Bench task and two arms. It produces no benchmark result.

Install the benchmark CLI

The harness requires Python 3.12 or newer and uv. This guide is pinned to Router commit cbe7584, so the source and manifest match the behavior described here:

git clone https://github.com/weave-os/router.git
cd router
git checkout cbe758442460ca68db8f4fe9837db087c50cf1e5
cd bench
uv sync --locked --extra harbor

Cloning the repository and syncing dependencies use the network. After that setup is complete, the planning command below builds and prints a local plan; it does not call the Router or model APIs or start Harbor jobs.

Print a one-task plan

This command compares the Router's router arm with a direct GPT-5.6 Luna control, using the benchmark's pinned smoke task:

uv run --locked --extra harbor weave-bench run terminal-bench-4 \
  --arms router,luna \
  --smoke \
  --dry-run

Representative output:

# terminal-bench-4 run_id=
# tasks=1 (manifest has 66); harbor=0.22.0 (published: 0.22.0) codex=0.150.0
...
--include-task-name terminal-bench/cad-model

The CLI generates the run ID. The important details are the selected task and the pinned versions, followed by the Harbor command for each arm.

What the plan means

  • One task, not 66: --smoke selects terminal-bench/cad-model from the 66-task manifest.
  • Two arms, two Harbor jobs: router sends requests through Weave Router's /beta policy; luna calls GPT-5.6 Luna directly. This is not a same-model comparison because the Router policy chooses a model per request.
  • Two attempts per arm: the pinned configuration sets two attempts and up to 12 concurrent tasks per job. For this one-task example, a real run is configured for up to four task attempts in total. An attempt can make multiple model requests, so that number is not an API-call count or a cost estimate.
  • No credentials in the plan: dry-run output shows the names of environment variables a real job would use, not their secret values. Keep credentials in the environment; do not paste them into a report.

--smoke only limits task selection. Remove --dry-run and the CLI launches the Harbor jobs, which can make model calls and incur compute and provider costs. Review the generated commands, budget, credentials, and sandbox configuration before launching. Treat a plan as a plan, never as benchmark evidence.

Sources

  • cmd_run returns before job launch when --dry-run is set
  • Benchmark package and Python version requirement
  • Terminal-Bench task, attempt, concurrency, and version pins
  • Router and direct Luna arm definitions
  • Weave Router benchmark methodology

This walkthrough explains the public CLI at the cited commit. No benchmark was launched and no new performance or cost result is claimed.

--smoke only limits task selection. Remove --dry-run and the CLI launches the Harbor jobs, which can make model calls and incur compute and provider costs. Review the generated commands, budget, credentials, and sandbox configuration before launching. Treat a plan as a plan, never as benchmark evidence.
